key_findings.finding: The mechanistic consequence of repeated alkalinization is biologically plausible: normal stratum-corneum pH is approximately 4.1–5.8, and acidity regulates lipid synthesis/organization, differentiation, desquamation and antimicrobial defense. Ceramide-generating beta-glucocerebrosidase and acidic sphingomyelinase require an acidic environment (reported optima around pH 5.6 and 4.5, respectively); raising pH can therefore transiently slow ceramide processing and barrier recovery, while removal of surface lipids can worsen barrier function. These enzyme/lipid conclusions are strongly supported by reviews, but direct human soap trials measuring enzyme activity are lacking.

key_findings.finding: Acidic pH also supports microbiome-related barrier defense: reviews state that acidic skin helps retain resident flora, whereas alkaline pH promotes bacterial dispersion. A 28-day randomized clinical evaluation of low-pH (<5) skincare in post-menopausal women found stable or increased microbiome diversity and a modest pH decrease with one product, suggesting that sustained acidic care does not inherently damage microbiome diversity; it did not test alkaline soap or establish a permanent pH reset.
